questions.stem: Your water utility's mains replacement programme runs with six two-person crews. The company-wide employee of the month scheme, a £150 voucher, has gone to the same crew leader twice this quarter. Since the second award, two crews have stopped lending spare fittings to one another and one has begun recording its own output separately so that it can be compared. Your sponsor believes the scheme is working, because the winning crew's productivity is up. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Ask the sponsor to adapt recognition on this programme so that it rewards results the crews produce jointly.
options.rationale: The scheme measures individuals inside work that only succeeds jointly, so it is buying one crew's output with the co-operation of the other five. Changing what gets noticed is the only lever that reaches the behaviour.

options.text: Leave the scheme in place, since the productivity figures show that it is motivating people.
options.rationale: This reads one crew's numbers as programme performance. It is the error of trusting the measure that improved while ignoring the co-operation that quietly stopped, which surfaces later as idle crews and borrowed fittings nobody has.

options.text: Rotate the award between crews so that each one receives it in turn.
options.rationale: Sharing by rota removes the competition and the meaning together. An award that arrives on a schedule tells nobody what they did well, and crews work out it is a rota within two months.

options.text: Suspend all recognition on the programme until the company has reviewed the scheme.
options.rationale: It treats recognition itself as the fault rather than the unit it is aimed at, withdrawing something people value and offering nothing in its place. It also hands the timing of any fix to a corporate review you do not control.

questions.explanation: Recognition changes behaviour in the direction it is aimed, so it has to be aimed at the unit that actually does the work. Where delivery depends on people helping each other, singling out individuals sets them competing, and the helping is the first thing to go — invisibly, because nobody announces that they have stopped. Read the second-order effect of any incentive before trusting the headline number it moved.
questions.mindset: Aim recognition at the unit that does the work, because behaviour follows whatever gets noticed.

questions.stem: A squad building control software for a brewery's bottling line is three sprints in. The equipment vendor has scheduled a run of two-hour technical calls, most of which cover commercial terms and delivery dates, with perhaps twenty minutes of content the developers actually need. The team has asked whether you could attend and bring back the parts that matter to them. Two developers have said they feel rude declining a supplier's invitation. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Attend the calls yourself and give the team a short summary of the parts that affect their work.
options.rationale: Absorbing coordination that does not need the team's craft is the job. It spends one person's time rather than six, and it removes the awkwardness of specialists having to decline a supplier themselves.

options.text: Ask the team to attend, since direct contact with the vendor stops information being filtered.
options.rationale: It applies a sound principle — go to the source — to a call that is mostly commercial. The error is treating all contact as equally valuable and paying six people's attention for twenty minutes of relevant content.

options.text: Ask the vendor to cancel the calls and send written updates instead.
options.rationale: This solves the team's problem by creating the vendor's, which they never agreed to. It also gives up the live conversation where delivery dates are actually negotiated, which is the part worth being in.

options.text: Set up a rota so that one developer attends each call on the team's behalf.
options.rationale: A rota spreads the cost instead of removing it, and each attendee arrives without the thread of the previous calls. It also leaves a developer representing the project on commercial matters they hold no mandate for.

questions.explanation: Shielding a team from work that is not theirs is not administrative tidying; it is a substantial part of leading delivery. The test is whose capability the activity genuinely requires: where it needs a mandate or an attention span rather than specialist hands, taking it on protects the scarcest thing the project has. Politeness towards a supplier is a cost the leader carries, not one the team should.
questions.mindset: Carry the coordination yourself so the team can spend its attention on the work only it can do.

questions.stem: One developer on your museum ticketing squad volunteers for every stretch item, picks up defects at weekends and has visibly raised the team's throughput over four sprints. At the last retrospective he said he was fine, just busy. Two other developers have started leaving the harder items alone, because he will take them anyway. Your delivery manager has asked you to hold him up as an example to the rest of the team. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Talk to him privately about the pattern, then rebalance who takes the harder items during planning.
options.rationale: It names two problems that are the same problem: one person absorbing the risk, and the rest of the team quietly stepping back. Fixing it in planning is what changes it, because planning is where the items get chosen.

options.text: Do as the delivery manager asks and hold him up as an example at the next team session.
options.rationale: Public praise for the behaviour is exactly what turns one person's habit into a team expectation. It also tells the other developers that stepping back has been endorsed, which is the opposite of the intent.

options.text: Leave it alone, since he is an adult who has said he is fine and the throughput figures are good.
options.rationale: It takes a two-word answer given in a group setting as informed consent. Throughput bought with weekends is borrowed, and the person carrying it is the least likely to say so in front of colleagues.

options.text: Give him the most complex work deliberately, since he is demonstrably the fastest at it.
options.rationale: It optimises this quarter's output by deepening a dependency on one person. The team's ability to do hard work then rests entirely on his continued availability, which nobody has guaranteed.

questions.explanation: Sustained over-commitment by one person is a fact about the team rather than a virtue in the individual: it silently changes what everybody else picks up, because people stop volunteering rather than announcing that they have. Output that rises while one person's hours rise is a loan, and the repayment falls due at the worst moment. The lever is the allocation mechanism, since that is where the behaviour is settled each iteration.
questions.mindset: Treat one person carrying more than their share as a fact about the team, not a fact about them.

questions.stem: On a ferry operator's terminal upgrade, a junior analyst produced the option appraisal that settled the berth redesign, working through three weeks of survey data. At yesterday's steering meeting the senior engineer presented it, said we looked at three options throughout, and answered every question himself. The sponsor thanked him warmly by name. The analyst was in the room and has said nothing about it since. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Tell the sponsor plainly who did the analysis, and put the analyst on the agenda to present the next one.
options.rationale: Correcting the record where the record was set is what makes it a correction, and the next presentation slot is the part that compounds. Visibility to a sponsor is an asset, and it was earned by somebody who did not receive it.

options.text: Correct the attribution in the meeting itself, as soon as the senior engineer has finished speaking.
options.rationale: The instinct is right and the venue is wrong. Correcting a colleague in front of the sponsor converts a fixable oversight into a public humiliation, and buys the analyst a resentful senior colleague she has to work with tomorrow.

options.text: Accept it, since presenting to steering is the senior engineer's role and the team's work is collective anyway.
options.rationale: It uses the language of collective delivery to launder one person's credit into another's. Shared work does not mean shared attribution, and the person who sees the difference most clearly is the one who was left out.

options.text: Raise it in the senior engineer's next performance review and say nothing to the sponsor.
options.rationale: It addresses the behaviour on a timescale that does nothing for the analyst, and leaves the sponsor holding a false picture of who can do this class of work. The record stays wrong where it matters.

questions.explanation: Attribution is a resource the leader controls, and it is worth far more to junior people than to senior ones. Where credit has landed in the wrong place, the useful response repairs it with the person whose opinion it affects and then changes the mechanism — who presents next time — rather than trusting goodwill to correct itself. Done privately and quickly, it costs the senior colleague nothing beyond a correction.
questions.mindset: Spend the credit you control on the people whose careers it can still move.

questions.stem: Your sponsor on a dairy plant upgrade has begun dropping into the delivery team's Monday planning meeting. Twice he has told individual engineers to prioritise items that were not on the agreed list, and both times the team reordered its week without telling you. He is enthusiastic and genuinely wants to help. The team now arrives at the meeting unsure whether the plan will survive the hour. Which two actions should the project manager take?

options.text: Speak to the sponsor privately about the effect his instructions are having, and agree how he takes part in future.
options.rationale: It treats the behaviour as well intentioned and fixable, which it is, and does so away from the team so that he can change without losing face. Agreeing the form of his participation keeps the access without the disruption.

options.text: Make explicit with the team how work enters the plan, so they know what to do when anyone asks them directly.
options.rationale: A team cannot decline a sponsor without a rule to point at. A stated route turns an awkward personal refusal into a procedural one, which is far easier for a junior engineer to hold.

options.text: Ask the sponsor to stop attending the planning meeting.
options.rationale: It removes the disruption by removing an engaged sponsor from the room where he can see the work. Access is hard to win back, and enthusiasm redirected elsewhere usually returns as pressure through the steering group.

options.text: Tell the team to keep to the agreed plan and disregard instructions that arrive from outside it.
options.rationale: It puts junior engineers in direct opposition to the sponsor and leaves them enforcing a boundary the project manager should be holding. They will not do it, and they are right not to.

options.text: Correct the sponsor in the meeting the next time he assigns work directly.
options.rationale: Doing it in front of the team wins the point and costs the relationship. It also makes the disagreement the team's news, rather than something already settled quietly between the two of you.

questions.explanation: A senior person disrupting a team's plan is usually a boundary problem rather than a discipline problem, and boundaries are the leader's to hold, not the team's. The pair that works addresses both sides at once: the individual's behaviour, privately, and the team's ability to route incoming requests, openly. A team given a rule can decline without it ever becoming personal.
questions.mindset: Hold the boundary yourself rather than leaving the team to defend a plan you agreed.

questions.stem: Your textiles group's ERP programme has six people in Leeds and three in Porto. Reviewing the last quarter, you notice the Porto engineers have received small self-contained tasks almost exclusively, while every piece of significant integration work has stayed in Leeds. Nobody decided this. The Leeds team lead explains that when something urgent lands it is quicker to turn to the person at the next desk. The Porto engineers have not complained. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Change how work is assigned so that allocation happens at a scheduled point rather than by whoever is nearest.
options.rationale: The cause is a mechanism rather than an attitude, so the fix has to be mechanical. Moving allocation to a moment when all nine are present removes the advantage proximity confers, and nobody has to be accused of anything.

options.text: Ask the Porto engineers to be more assertive about the work they want.
options.rationale: It places the cost of fixing an allocation problem on the people disadvantaged by it, and asks them to challenge decisions taken in a room they are not in. Even if they try, the mechanism is untouched.

options.text: Reassure the Leeds lead that the split is a practical response to urgency, and watch it for another quarter.
options.rationale: It accepts an explanation as a justification. Another quarter of the same pattern hardens into a real capability gap, which is then cited as the reason the split has to continue.

options.text: Move the integration work to Porto for the next quarter to even out the balance.
options.rationale: Correcting an imbalance by imposing its mirror leaves the underlying mechanism intact and adds disruption. It also treats the outcome as the target, when the way work is chosen is the thing that needs to change.

questions.explanation: Where work is allocated informally it flows towards whoever is easiest to ask, and distance is the strongest filter there is. The resulting pattern looks like a judgement about capability but was never a judgement at all, which is why arguing about intentions gets nowhere and offends everybody. Change the moment and the method by which work is handed out, and the pattern changes without a confrontation.
questions.mindset: When an unfair pattern emerges from nobody's decision, change the mechanism rather than the people.

questions.stem: You told your seed-research data squad that tooling choices were theirs to make. They spent two weeks evaluating options, ran a careful comparison and chose a platform costing €40,000 a year — far above the €10,000 you can approve, and above what the programme holds. You now have to refuse. The team is frustrated and one developer has said out loud that there was no point doing the evaluation. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Acknowledge that the limit should have been stated, give them the budget figure, and ask them to decide again inside it.
options.rationale: It puts the failure where it belongs and preserves the authority instead of withdrawing it. A boundary supplied late is still a boundary the team can work with, and re-deciding inside it is what proves the delegation was real.

options.text: Approve the choice and find the money elsewhere in the programme so that the team's decision stands.
options.rationale: It rescues one decision by breaking a budget the project manager is accountable for, and teaches that limits yield to sufficient commitment. Every later evaluation will be built on that assumption.

options.text: Refuse the platform and select an affordable tool yourself, to save the team any further time.
options.rationale: It converts a missing constraint into a withdrawn decision. The team learns that autonomy lasts precisely until it produces an inconvenient answer, which is worse than never having been offered it.

options.text: Escalate to the sponsor for additional budget on the strength of the team's evaluation.
options.rationale: It spends sponsor credit to avoid admitting an omission, and makes the team's authority contingent on somebody else's generosity. If the answer comes back no, the team is exactly here again with a delay attached.

questions.explanation: Delegated authority is defined by its constraints, and an unstated constraint is the delegator's error rather than the team's. The repair is to supply what was missing and hand the decision back, because taking it away instead teaches that empowerment is conditional on agreeing with the leader. Every handover of a decision should carry its limits — money, time, reversibility — at the moment it is handed over.
questions.mindset: Give the boundaries with the decision, because authority without limits is not authority you can honour.

questions.stem: Your veterinary diagnostics team agreed in January that everyone would work from the laboratory office three days a week, because the analysts and the developers need each other constantly. Two developers have quietly settled into one day. Nobody has raised it. Three others have begun mentioning, half jokingly, that they are the only ones who bother coming in. The agreement is drifting and the joking has an edge to it. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Take it back to the whole team: re-establish what the office days are for, and what each person is committing to.
options.rationale: The agreement belongs to the team, so its renewal does too. Re-anchoring it on purpose rather than attendance gives people a reason to keep it, and settles the resentment by making the expectation explicit again.

options.text: Speak to the two developers individually and ask them to return to three days.
options.rationale: It treats a decayed team norm as two people's misconduct. Even if they comply, everybody else has watched the agreement need policing, and the next drift will also wait for the project manager to notice it.

options.text: Drop the requirement, since the work has evidently carried on without it.
options.rationale: It reads the absence of a visible failure as proof the contact was never needed, and rewards the drift. The analysts who relied on being able to turn round and ask something are the ones who pay for it.

options.text: Send a reminder of the agreement to the whole team without naming anyone.
options.rationale: An unaddressed reminder is read carefully by the people already complying and ignored by those who are not. It signals that the project manager has noticed but would rather not have the conversation.

questions.explanation: Team agreements decay quietly, and the damage usually arrives as resentment among the people still keeping them rather than as any failure of the work. Renewal belongs in the forum that made the agreement, because an expectation enforced person by person stops being a shared commitment and becomes a rule the leader has to police. Ask what an agreement is for before asking whether it is being kept.
questions.mindset: Renew a team agreement with the team, or watch it become a rule you alone have to police.

questions.stem: Three mistakes have surfaced on your substation replacement programme within the same month. One was made by a capable engineer attempting an unfamiliar task for the first time. One was the third occurrence of the same error by an engineer who has twice had clear and specific feedback about it. One was made by a technician who followed the written procedure exactly and still produced a wrong result. Match each to the response it calls for. One choice is not used.

prompts.text: A capable engineer, working on an unfamiliar task for the first time, makes an error that review catches.
An engineer repeats the same error a third time, having twice received clear and specific feedback.
A technician follows the written procedure exactly, and the procedure produces a wrong result.

options.text: Coach through the error and have the same person redo the work
options.rationale: A first error on unfamiliar work is the ordinary cost of somebody learning something new. Handing the work back after coaching is what turns the mistake into capability rather than into a task that quietly becomes someone else's.

options.text: Set the expectation formally and in writing, with the consequence of a further repeat
options.rationale: Repetition after specific feedback has already exhausted coaching. Formalising it is fairer than another informal chat, because it tells the person exactly where they stand while there is still time to change.

options.text: Change the procedure and take no action in respect of the individual
options.rationale: Where correct execution produces a wrong result, the defect sits in the instruction. Acting on the person would punish compliance and leave the trap in place for whoever meets it next.

options.text: Refer the matter to human resources for formal investigation
options.rationale: Not used. Investigation is for conduct — dishonesty, safety breaches, the treatment of colleagues — rather than for errors of inexperience, repetition or process. Reaching for it in any of these three would be disproportionate and would teach the team to hide mistakes.

questions.explanation: The right response to a mistake depends entirely on its cause, and these three causes demand opposite things: inexperience needs teaching, repetition after feedback needs a clear boundary, and faithful execution of a bad instruction needs the instruction fixed. Applying one habitual response across all of them makes a leader either indulgent or unjust, depending which habit they have. Diagnose first, and the same person can be coached one month and held to account the next without any inconsistency.
questions.mindset: Ask what caused a mistake before deciding what it deserves.

questions.stem: A release of your cinema chain's loyalty platform failed on Saturday night and tills fell back to manual for four hours. The cause was a configuration change made by a junior engineer following a runbook that had not been updated since March. Two colleagues reviewed the change and neither noticed. Your sponsor has told you he wants the engineer off the project by Monday. Which two actions should the project manager take?

options.text: Tell the sponsor that this was a process failure, set out what is being changed, and decline the removal.
options.rationale: The runbook and the review both failed, and taking out the last person in the chain repairs neither. Saying so to an angry sponsor is the part that takes nerve, and it decides whether anyone reports the next near miss.

options.text: Run a review of the failure with the team that examines the runbook and the review step rather than the individual.
options.rationale: It puts the investigation where the causes actually are and produces changes that outlast any one engineer. Involving the team is also what stops the review being read as a hunt for somebody to hand over.

options.text: Move the engineer to another workstream to restore the sponsor's confidence.
options.rationale: It buys one weekend of calm at the price of the team's willingness to touch anything risky. Everybody watching learns that whoever holds the spanner carries the whole system's failure.

options.text: Agree to the removal in the meeting and quietly keep the engineer on the team.
options.rationale: Managing a sponsor by saying what he wants to hear leaves an unresolved disagreement and a discoverable untruth. When it surfaces, what is lost is the project manager's credibility on every future assurance.

options.text: Ask the engineer to apologise to the sponsor personally.
options.rationale: It stages accountability at the wrong level and puts a junior person in front of an angry executive for a fault that was mostly not hers. The team reads it correctly, as blame flowing downhill.

questions.explanation: When a failure passes through several controls before it reaches production, the controls are the finding and the last person in the chain is an accident of the rota. The leader's task at that moment is to hold the pressure at their own level rather than passing it down, because a team that watches a colleague sacrificed will hide the next problem until it is unmissable. Accountability belongs with whoever is able to change the system.
questions.mindset: Take the pressure at your own level; a team that sees blame flow downhill stops telling you things.

questions.stem: The overnight incident rota for your pharmacy chain's stock system exists on paper, but in practice one engineer takes almost every call. He is good at it, he is proud of it, and the team thanks him in every retrospective. Over six months the routing has hardened: alerts now go straight to his phone and two newer engineers have never handled a live incident. He says he prefers it this way. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Change the alert routing and pair a second engineer with him on each incident, saying openly why the change is being made.
options.rationale: It moves the dependency without withdrawing the standing he has earned, which is the part most likely to make him resist. Pairing builds a second and third responder using incidents that are going to happen anyway.

options.text: Formalise the arrangement by naming him incident owner and paying an on-call allowance.
options.rationale: It converts an accidental single point of failure into a designed one and pays for the privilege. The retrospective thanks are already cementing this; a title and an allowance make it far harder to unwind later.

options.text: Tell him to stop taking the calls so that the others are forced to learn.
options.rationale: It removes the safety net before the replacements exist, and reads as a punishment aimed at the person who has been covering. The first bad night reverses the decision and the dependency returns stronger.

options.text: Recruit a second experienced engineer so that the load is shared.
options.rationale: It treats a distribution problem as a headcount problem, on a timescale of months. The routing and the recognition loop are untouched, so the new joiner arrives in a team where incidents already have an owner.

questions.explanation: A team's dependence on one person rarely arrives by decision; it accumulates through routing, gratitude and everyone else's quiet relief. That makes it a leadership problem rather than a rota problem, because the two forces holding it in place — convenience and praise — are both within the leader's control. Rebuild the capability using the events that occur anyway, and say plainly that the change is about the system rather than about the person who has been carrying it.
questions.mindset: When gratitude is reinforcing a dependency, change the routing before the dependency becomes a design.

questions.stem: You have led an eleven-person team on a wind farm cabling project for five months. All your contact with them happens in the weekly team meeting and in the shared channel. Preparing performance inputs, you realise you could describe the working lives of four people in detail and the other seven barely at all — and that the four are the ones who speak up in meetings. Nothing has gone wrong. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Start regular individual conversations with each of the eleven, and hold them even when nothing is wrong.
options.rationale: Individual contact is the only channel in which the quieter seven can raise something small. Holding the sessions when nothing is wrong is what makes them usable later, because a meeting that happens only in a crisis becomes a signal in itself.

options.text: Circulate an anonymous team survey to find out how the quieter seven are getting on.
options.rationale: A survey buys information while avoiding the relationship that would have produced it, and anonymity guarantees nothing can be followed up. It asks people to write down what they have never been asked in person.

options.text: Ask the four you know well to keep you informed about how their colleagues are doing.
options.rationale: It formalises a two-tier team and makes seven people the subject of second-hand reporting. Anything sensitive would have to travel through a colleague, which is exactly why it would not travel at all.

options.text: Set aside time in the weekly team meeting to invite the quieter members to contribute.
options.rationale: It tries to close an individual-contact gap inside the forum that created it. Being invited to speak in front of ten colleagues raises the cost of speaking rather than lowering it.

questions.explanation: Information about a team distributes itself unevenly by default, arriving from whoever is comfortable in whichever venue the leader happens to use. Where the only forum is a group one, a leader ends up knowing the confident well and everyone else by inference, and the gap stays invisible until something goes wrong inside it. Routine individual contact is a structural correction rather than a courtesy, and its value comes precisely from being routine rather than triggered by concern.
questions.mindset: Make time with each person routine, so nobody has to create an occasion in order to tell you something.

questions.stem: A business analyst on your insurance broker's policy administration programme tells you she wants to move into project management and asks whether you would help her learn. The programme is entering its busiest quarter, you are already stretched, and there is no formal mentoring scheme in the organisation. Your instinct is to say yes but start after go-live in four months. She has clearly thought carefully about how to ask. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Say yes now and start with something small and real, such as her running the weekly risk review and debriefing with you after it.
options.rationale: Development scheduled after the busy period rarely happens, because the next busy period is already forming. Attaching it to work that exists anyway costs almost nothing and gives her something concrete to be judged on.

options.text: Explain that the next four months are unusually demanding and commit to starting properly after go-live.
options.rationale: It sounds responsible and is the most common way development quietly dies. What she hears is a deferral, and the honest reading is that there will always be another go-live.

options.text: Refer her to human resources so that she can be entered into a formal development programme.
options.rationale: It converts a personal request into a process that may take months and may not exist. The one thing she actually asked for — access to somebody doing the job — is the thing a referral cannot supply.

options.text: Hand her a set of project management tasks to take on alongside her analysis work.
options.rationale: Passing over tasks without the reasoning behind them produces an assistant rather than a project manager, and adds load in the hardest quarter. The learning sits in the judgement, not in the administration.

questions.explanation: Developing people is not a separate activity to be funded once delivery goes quiet; it happens inside the work that is running anyway, which is why a busy period is a poor reason to defer it. A useful response to a development request is small, specific and immediate, because that is what tests whether the interest is real on both sides. A promise dated after the next milestone is usually a polite refusal that both parties can pretend was a yes.
questions.mindset: Start development inside the work you already have, because the quiet quarter you are waiting for never arrives.

questions.stem: Three status rounds running, your hotel group's booking migration has been reported green by the workstream lead. A tester mentions in passing that two of those weeks were known internally to be at serious risk. You then remember that when the same lead reported amber in June, you questioned the figure sharply in front of the programme board and asked him to justify it on the spot. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Tell the lead what you have concluded about your own reaction in June, and ask him what would make an honest amber safe to file.
options.rationale: The behaviour was trained, and naming the training is the fastest way to untrain it. Asking him to describe what safety would look like moves the conversation from apology to a change that can actually be observed.

options.text: Address the misreporting with the lead as a performance matter and require evidence behind every future status.
options.rationale: It punishes a symptom the leader's own reaction produced, and adds surveillance on top. Evidence requirements yield better-decorated greens, because the incentive to report green has not moved at all.

options.text: Report the concealment to the programme board before the true position emerges from somewhere else.
options.rationale: Getting the news out first protects the project manager and lands the lead with a failure that is partly the project manager's own. The team reads the sequence accurately, and the next warning reaches nobody.

options.text: Commission an independent assurance review of status reporting across all workstreams.
options.rationale: It answers one broken relationship with a general control, at cost and delay. Assurance can detect an optimistic report but cannot make it safe for somebody to file a pessimistic one.

questions.explanation: Status is a behaviour, and it responds to whatever happened to the last person who reported bad news. Where reporting has drifted optimistic, the first place to look is the leader's own reaction, because that is usually both the cause and the only variable they can change immediately. Controls stacked on top of a fear of reporting produce more convincing reports rather than more accurate ones, and the cost of the fear is paid at the moment recovery is still possible.
questions.mindset: Before asking why nobody told you, ask what happened to the last person who did.

questions.stem: Your telecoms self-service app squad raises three blockers in the same week and, out of habit, expects you to clear all three. In fact each belongs somewhere different: one sits entirely inside the team's own gift, one needs authority nobody on the team holds, and one needs a senior person to stop doing something. Complete each sentence with the response that fits. One choice is not used.

prompts.text: The code review queue has grown because the team's own rule requires two reviewers on every change, and the team is free to change that rule. The project manager should
Work has stopped for want of a software licence that only a director may authorise, and nobody on the team can raise the request. The project manager should
A marketing director keeps contacting engineers directly to reorder their priorities, and did so twice last week. The project manager should

options.text: put it to the team to solve at its next retrospective, and stay out of the answer
options.rationale: The constraint is a rule the team wrote and can rewrite. Solving it for them removes both the ownership and the practice of noticing their own bottlenecks, and it spends leader time on the one blocker that did not need any.

options.text: obtain the authorisation personally, using access the team does not have
options.rationale: The blocker is made of authority, which is the one currency the team cannot mint. Hesitating here in the name of self-organisation leaves people idle over something only the project manager could ever have moved.

options.text: take the conversation with the director on themselves and shield the team from it
options.rationale: Asking engineers to hold a boundary against a director asks them to risk a relationship they cannot afford to lose. The seniority mismatch is the whole problem, and the leader is the person who can absorb it.

options.text: log it on the impediment board and review it at the fortnightly programme meeting
options.rationale: Not used. Logging is how a blocker is tracked rather than how it is cleared, and each of these three has an owner who could act today. Routing any of them to a fortnightly forum adds a fortnight to something that is stopping work now.

questions.explanation: Removing impediments does not mean removing all of them personally; the useful question is what the blocker needs that the team does not have. Where it needs only a decision the team is entitled to take, solving it costs them the ownership and costs the leader time that the other blockers require. Where it needs authority, access or a difficult conversation with someone senior, the leader is the only available actor and hesitating is not humility.
questions.mindset: Clear what the team cannot reach, and hand back what it can.

questions.stem: Two technicians must hold a three-day vendor certification before they may commission the new life-support controllers at your aquarium. The only course running before commissioning falls in the week you had set aside for final tank trials, and your sponsor has called the certification a nice-to-have that can follow handover. Without it the vendor will not permit the technicians to configure the units at all. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Move the tank trials, send both technicians on the course, and show the sponsor why commissioning depends on it.
options.rationale: This certification is not development in the general sense; it is a gate the vendor imposes on the work itself. Presenting it as a prerequisite rather than a benefit is what changes how the sponsor weighs the trade.

options.text: Follow the sponsor's steer and schedule the certification for after handover.
options.rationale: It accepts a judgement made without the vendor's condition in view. Handover then arrives with two technicians who are contractually barred from touching the units they are supposed to operate.

options.text: Have the vendor commission the units and let the technicians observe during the visit.
options.rationale: It buys the milestone and leaves the capability behind. The aquarium then depends on the vendor for every later configuration change, at a recurring cost far above three days of course fees.

options.text: Send one technician to the course and have him brief the other on his return.
options.rationale: A briefing is not a certification, and the vendor's permission does not transfer between people. It also concentrates the entire capability in one person to save three days.

questions.explanation: Some training is a benefit and some is a precondition of the work, and the two have to be argued for in completely different ways. Where a supplier, a regulator or a licence makes competence a condition of proceeding, it belongs in the schedule as a dependency rather than in a development plan as an aspiration. A sponsor's view usually changes the moment an item stops being a good thing for people and becomes a thing without which the work cannot legally or contractually happen.
questions.mindset: Schedule capability the work requires as a dependency, not as a benefit to be squeezed in later.

questions.stem: Your bakery chain's ordering app squad sits together at four desks and has asked to drop the daily standup. They say that by the time it starts they already know what everyone is doing, and the fifteen minutes is spent restating it. They are delivering well and the request is polite and unanimous. Your delivery manager has told you that standups are non-negotiable across the department. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Agree to drop it, ask the team what will replace the signal it was giving, and review the change at the next retrospective.
options.rationale: The team owns how it works and a ceremony producing nothing is spending real time. Asking what replaces the signal keeps the purpose while letting the ritual go, and the review makes the change reversible rather than final.

options.text: Keep the standup, because it is a required part of how the organisation delivers.
options.rationale: It defends the ritual instead of the purpose, in front of a team that has just shown it understands the difference. The standup survives; the team's belief that its opinion carries weight does not.

options.text: Drop the standup with no replacement, since the team plainly coordinates well without it.
options.rationale: It grants the request without preserving what the meeting was for. Sitting together covers coordination today, but nothing now surfaces an impediment or a stalled item, and the gap shows up weeks later.

options.text: Replace the standup with a short written update sent to you each morning.
options.rationale: It turns a team coordination event into a reporting line to the project manager. The team loses the only moment it had to hear from each other and gains an obligation to inform you.

questions.explanation: A practice earns its place by the signal it produces rather than by its position in a framework, and a team that can state precisely what a ceremony is failing to produce has already done the analysis. The judgement is whether the underlying need has genuinely gone or merely become invisible, and keeping the need while dropping the form is almost always available. Changes to a team's own way of working should be reversible and reviewed rather than permanent and unexamined.
questions.mindset: Defend what a practice is for, and let the team change the shape it arrives in.

questions.stem: A senior surveyor on your port container terminal project applied for the team lead role six weeks ago and did not get it; the post went to an external candidate. Since then his work has arrived late three times, though its quality is unchanged, and he has told two colleagues the project is going nowhere. He has said nothing to you. In every previous month he was your most reliable performer. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Meet him, name what you have observed alongside the decision he is probably still carrying, and ask him directly.
options.rationale: The timing points to a cause that is not capability, and naming it is what makes the conversation honest rather than procedural. Asking rather than asserting leaves room for him to say something different, which matters if the reading is wrong.

options.text: Open a performance management process on the strength of the three late deliveries.
options.rationale: It applies a capability remedy to a motivation problem. The lapses are real, but a process built to test whether he can do the work will confirm that he can, and will harden the grievance while doing it.

options.text: Leave it, since the quality of his work is unaffected and the reaction will fade in time.
options.rationale: It waits out a disengagement that colleagues can already see. Two of them have now heard from the most respected person on the team that the project is going nowhere, and that view does not fade quietly.

options.text: Offer him the next team lead vacancy that arises, to settle the matter.
options.rationale: It makes a promise about a decision the project manager may not control, and buys present compliance with a future appointment. If the vacancy never comes, or he is again not the strongest candidate, the damage is far worse.

questions.explanation: When a reliable performer's behaviour changes sharply while their capability has not, the cause is usually something that happened to them rather than something they are unable to do. Performance machinery is built for capability, and pointing it at a grievance confirms the person's belief that nobody is listening. The conversation to have is the direct one, early, with the likely cause named aloud, because an unspoken reason cannot be addressed and does not decay on its own.
questions.mindset: When performance drops but capability has not, look for what happened rather than for what is missing.

questions.stem: Two engineers left your glass plant manufacturing execution system programme last month and two replacements started on Monday. Headcount is unchanged, so your sponsor expects output to be unchanged and has said so in the steering minutes. Your team lead expects the next two iterations to be noticeably slower, because the leavers held most of the plant floor knowledge. Which two actions should the project manager take?

options.text: Set the sponsor's expectation now, giving the depth and length of the dip and the point at which output should recover.
options.rationale: A dip explained in advance is a plan; the same dip explained afterwards is an excuse. Giving the shape and the recovery point turns it into something the sponsor can hold you to, rather than a vague warning.

options.text: Reduce what the team commits to for the next two iterations and pair each new engineer with an experienced one.
options.rationale: It makes the forecast true instead of hoping against it, and spends the reduced capacity on the transfer that causes the recovery. Pairing puts the learning inside work that has to be done anyway.

options.text: Hold the committed scope, so that the team is not given permission to slow down.
options.rationale: It treats a capability gap as a motivation problem. The team meets the number by cutting the invisible things — testing, review, the new engineers' questions — and the cost returns later as defects.

options.text: Give the two new engineers a separate workstream so that they do not disrupt the established pair.
options.rationale: It protects short-term throughput by creating a second team with no plant floor knowledge and no route to acquiring any. The isolation guarantees the same dip recurs whenever those two are needed on the main work.

options.text: Ask the two leavers to stay available for questions from their new employers.
options.rationale: It builds the recovery on goodwill from people who no longer work for you and have their own new jobs to learn. It also postpones the moment the team has to become self-sufficient, which is the moment recovery starts.

questions.explanation: Replacing people is not the same as replacing capability, and flat headcount hides the difference from anyone reading a resourcing report. Two things must happen together: the expectation of the people watching is reset in advance, and the team's committed load is cut far enough that transfer can actually take place. Doing only the first gives you an informed audience watching a team fail; doing only the second gives you a recovering team and a sponsor who believes it is underperforming.
questions.mindset: Say the dip is coming before it arrives, and make room for the transfer that ends it.

questions.stem: Your distillery bottling squad has decided to build its own scheduling component rather than buy the one you would have chosen. The decision sits inside the remit you gave them, the reasoning is sound if optimistic, and you think buying is the better answer. The choice is reversible at moderate cost for about six weeks, after which it is not. You have not yet told them what you think. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Give them your view once with your reasoning, let the decision stand, and agree what evidence would tell everyone it was wrong.
options.rationale: Withholding an opinion is not neutrality when you hold relevant experience, and overriding is not leadership when the decision was theirs. The agreed review point uses the reversibility window, which is the only thing here that expires.

options.text: Say nothing, since the decision is theirs and offering a view would put a thumb on the scale.
options.rationale: It mistakes abdication for restraint. The team is entitled to the leader's experience, and discovering months later that you disagreed all along costs more trust than disagreeing openly ever would.

options.text: Overrule the decision, since you are accountable for the outcome and you believe buying is correct.
options.rationale: It reclaims a genuinely delegated decision over a judgement call rather than a breached constraint. From then on every decision inside their remit arrives at your desk for approval, which is the real price.

options.text: Refer the question to the architecture group so that an independent party settles it.
options.rationale: It outsources a disagreement you are perfectly able to have directly, and dresses an override in somebody else's authority. The team reads the referral accurately, as a route to the answer you preferred.

questions.explanation: Delegating a decision means living with an answer you would not have chosen, provided it sits within the constraints and the people making it are competent to do so. What the leader still owes is an honest view, offered once with reasons, and a review point tied to the moment the choice stops being reversible. Silence deprives a team of expertise and reversal deprives it of authority, and only the first of those can be repaired cheaply.
questions.mindset: Say what you think once, then let a delegated decision be theirs — and agree in advance what would change it.

questions.stem: Your sponsor on a packaging print project wants a number today for what the team will deliver in the coming four-week iteration. The team is six engineers on five-day weeks. Six days of leave are already booked across the group, and the team spends a fifth of its remaining time supporting the live estate. You intend to hold back a tenth of what is left as contingency before you commit to anything. Work the figures through.

blanks.label: Gross capacity for the iteration, in person-days
blanks.rationale: Six engineers across four five-day weeks is 6 x 20 = 120 person-days. This is the figure a headcount report shows and the only one of the three that requires no knowledge of the team.

blanks.label: Capacity left after booked leave and support duties, in person-days
blanks.rationale: Subtract the six booked leave days first, giving 114, then remove the fifth spent on support: 114 x 0.8 = 91.2 person-days. Order matters, because the support share applies to time the team is actually present.

blanks.label: The figure to commit to after holding a tenth back, in person-days
blanks.rationale: Holding back a tenth of 91.2 leaves 91.2 x 0.9 = 82.08, so about 82.1 person-days. The contingency is not pessimism; it is the space in which the unplanned work of any four-week period lands.

blanks.label: Name the planning error of offering the sponsor the first of these three figures
blanks.rationale: Quoting 120 treats every paid day as a delivering day, which no team has ever achieved. The gap between gross capacity and available capacity is where over-commitment is manufactured, one reasonable-sounding number at a time.

questions.explanation: Headcount multiplied by working days is a payroll figure, not a delivery figure, and the distance between the two is made of leave, support, meetings and the unplanned. A commitment made at gross capacity fails without anyone doing anything wrong, which is the worst kind of failure to lead a team through because there is no lesson in it. Deriving the number in front of the sponsor also changes the conversation from haggling over a promise to examining the deductions.
questions.mindset: Commit from what the team actually has, and show the sponsor the deductions rather than the conclusion.

questions.stem: Your geospatial software team began the quarter with twelve people. Three left during it and three replacements have now started. Your organisation's own figures say a new joiner takes thirty working days to reach full productivity and produces on average forty per cent of full output over that period. Your delivery manager has told the steering group that the team is back to full strength because the headcount has been restored. Work out what the quarter actually cost.

blanks.label: Turnover for the quarter, as a percentage of the opening headcount
blanks.rationale: Three leavers against an opening headcount of twelve is 3 / 12 = 25 per cent in a single quarter. Expressing it as a rate rather than as three people is what makes it comparable with other teams and other quarters.

blanks.label: Output lost per replacement during the ramp-up, in person-days
blanks.rationale: Across thirty days at forty per cent output, the shortfall is 30 x 0.6 = 18 person-days per joiner. The days are worked and paid for; the difference is what does not arrive as delivered work.

blanks.label: Total output lost across all three replacements, in person-days
blanks.rationale: Three joiners at 18 person-days each is 54 person-days, and that is before the time experienced colleagues spend answering their questions. A headcount report shows none of this because the headcount never changed.

blanks.label: Name the shortfall a new joiner produces before reaching full productivity
blanks.rationale: The gap between a person arriving and a person contributing fully is the ramp-up, and it is a real cost even though nobody invoices for it. Naming it is what lets a leader put it in a forecast rather than absorb it as an unexplained slowdown.

questions.explanation: Headcount measures presence and says nothing about capability, which is why a restored headcount is routinely reported as a restored team. The quantities that matter are the rate at which people leave and the time each replacement takes to become productive, and both are knowable in advance rather than discovered afterwards. Putting a number on the ramp is what converts an argument about whether the team is trying hard enough into a schedule conversation about when capability returns.
questions.mindset: Count capability rather than headcount, because the two only agree on the day nobody has moved.

questions.stem: Your mining haulage systems programme has had a team of eight working fifty-hour weeks for nine weeks to hold a commissioning date. Your own organisation's studies of sustained overtime conclude that the additional hours yield full output for roughly the first two weeks and effectively none after that, because errors and rework rise to absorb them. Your sponsor is now proposing four more weeks of the same. Work out what the nine weeks bought.

blanks.label: Additional hours worked per week across the whole team
blanks.rationale: Eight people working ten hours beyond a forty-hour week is 8 x 10 = 80 additional hours every week. Stated per team rather than per person, the figure is large enough that people stop treating it as a small favour.

blanks.label: Total additional hours across the nine weeks
blanks.rationale: Nine weeks at 80 additional hours is 720 hours, or roughly ninety working days of human effort. This is the size of the investment the programme has already made without ever recording a decision to make it.

blanks.label: Additional hours that produced output, on the stated assumption
blanks.rationale: Only the first two weeks yield, so 2 x 80 = 160 hours of the 720 produced anything. The remaining 560 hours were worked, paid and absorbed by the errors and rework they generated.

blanks.label: In one word, what those remaining 560 hours bought the programme
blanks.rationale: On the organisation's own figures the answer is nothing, which is the number that makes the case to the sponsor. Arguing against overtime on grounds of fairness invites a debate; arguing on grounds of yield does not.

questions.explanation: Sustained overtime is borrowing rather than earning, and the repayment arrives as defects, attrition and the slow disappearance of everything a team does that nobody measures. A leader arguing against an extension is usually heard as protecting people at the expense of the date, which is why the yield calculation matters: it reframes the request as a proposal to spend effort that the organisation's own evidence says will not arrive. Fatigue is a delivery variable, and it belongs in the same conversation as scope and schedule.
questions.mindset: Price overtime by what it yields, not by the hours it adds, and say so before the next block is agreed.

questions.stem: Three moments arise in the same afternoon on your agricultural co-operative's grain intake product. A developer asks how to approach something she has done successfully many times. A second is about to configure a weighbridge interface in a way that would breach the calibration rule the site is inspected against. A third has just finished a difficult piece of work well and clearly does not realise it. Match each moment to the response it calls for. One choice is not used.

prompts.text: A developer asks how to approach a task she has completed successfully many times before.
A developer is about to act in a way that would breach the calibration rule the site is inspected against.
A developer has just completed a difficult piece of work well and does not appear to know it.

options.text: Ask her what she would do, and back the answer she gives
options.rationale: She has the experience and is asking for reassurance rather than instruction. Answering would take the decision back and teach her to check with you next time; asking hands her the confidence along with the task.

options.text: Tell her not to proceed, plainly and immediately, and explain the reason afterwards
options.rationale: Where a breach is imminent and externally enforced, the cost of a coaching question is a non-conformance that cannot be undone. Directness is not a failure of style here; delaying it would be.

options.text: Say specifically what was good about the work, and say it within the day
options.rationale: Unrecognised good work teaches a person that quality is invisible, and general praise teaches nothing at all. Naming the specific thing is what makes it repeatable, and saying it quickly is what connects it to the work.

options.text: Note the observation and raise it at her next formal performance review
options.rationale: Not used. Deferring destroys the value of all three: coaching arrives after the decision is made, the calibration breach has already been inspected, and praise six weeks late is a record rather than a signal.

questions.explanation: Leadership style is chosen by the moment rather than by habit or by the seniority of the person in front of you, and the cost of the wrong choice differs each time. Asking where you should have told allows an irreversible breach; telling where you should have asked removes a decision somebody was ready to make. The variables worth reading quickly are how reversible the situation is and whether the person needs capability, permission or acknowledgement.
questions.mindset: Choose the response the moment needs, not the one your style prefers.

questions.stem: Your timber mill automation programme runs across four sites and three frictions have become chronic. New joiners take weeks to work out how the team operates. Nobody is certain who may approve spending under €500, so every request waits for you. The same two voices dominate every design session while the rest of the group stays silent. Match each friction to the artefact or agreement that addresses it. One choice is not used.

prompts.text: New joiners take weeks to work out how the team operates, and learn it by making mistakes.
Nobody is certain who may approve spending under €500, so every request waits for the project manager.
The same two voices dominate every design session and the rest of the group stays silent.

options.text: A written team working agreement, kept current by the team itself
options.rationale: The knowledge exists but lives only in people's heads, so every joiner rediscovers it by trial and error. Writing it down turns weeks of inference into a half-hour read, and the team maintaining it is what stops it becoming fiction.

options.text: A delegated authority schedule naming who may approve what, and up to what value
options.rationale: The bottleneck is ambiguity rather than caution, and ambiguity always resolves upward. Naming the limits removes the project manager from a class of decisions nobody ever needed them for.

options.text: A facilitation rota and a timeboxed agenda for design sessions
options.rationale: Dominance in a meeting is a structural result of who runs it and how loosely it runs. Rotating the facilitator and bounding the time changes the structure, so nobody has to be told to talk less.

options.text: A responsibility assignment matrix covering every task on the programme
options.rationale: Not used. A task-level matrix is heavy, goes stale within weeks, and answers a question none of these frictions asks. Two of them concern authority and voice rather than task ownership, and the third is about induction.

questions.explanation: Chronic friction usually indicates a missing artefact rather than a shortage of goodwill, and each kind of friction has its own small durable fix. Induction problems want something written, authority problems want limits named, and participation problems want the structure of the meeting changed. Reaching instead for more of the leader's personal attention appears to work while the leader is present and reappears the moment they are not.
questions.mindset: Answer recurring friction with a small durable artefact, not with more of your own attention.

questions.stem: Six months ago you told your chocolate packaging line squad that anyone, at any level, could stop a release if they were not confident in it. Last Thursday a graduate engineer used that right and the release slipped a day. Nothing went wrong afterwards and her reasoning was sound if cautious. This morning the operations manager asked you to restrict the right to senior engineers only. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Keep the right as it stands, back the graduate openly, and offer the operations manager release data after another quarter.
options.rationale: Authority withdrawn the first time it costs something was never authority. Backing her openly is what tells everyone the rule is real, and offering evidence later answers the manager's concern without conceding the principle today.

options.text: Restrict the right to senior engineers, who are better placed to judge the risk.
options.rationale: It sounds like calibration and operates as a repeal. The person closest to a defect is frequently the most junior, and the change tells them plainly that their doubt is not worth a day of the schedule.

options.text: Keep the right but require your countersignature before any release is stopped.
options.rationale: A right that needs the project manager's approval is a request. It also places the leader in the path of a decision whose entire value lies in being available immediately and without permission.

options.text: Withdraw the right and rely on the existing automated test gates to catch problems.
options.rationale: It replaces human judgement at the point of doubt with checks the release had already passed. Gates catch what they were written to catch; the graduate stopped for something nobody had thought to write.

questions.explanation: A right to stop work is worth exactly as much as its usability without negotiation, so the first exercise of it — especially a cautious one that proves unnecessary — is the moment that decides whether it exists at all. Restricting it once a cost has been incurred tells the whole team what the original announcement was worth. Granting authority means expecting to pay for it at least once and treating that payment as the price of the rule rather than as evidence against it.
questions.mindset: Expect to pay for the authority you grant, and pay without renegotiating it.

questions.stem: You manage a dockyard refit from a head office ninety minutes away. Everything you know about the two field crews arrives through the site supervisor's Friday report, which has recorded morale as good for eleven weeks running. Over the same period rework on the hull sections has risen every month and two experienced fitters have resigned. You have met four of the twenty-three people on site. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Spend regular time on site, walking the work and talking to the crews without the supervisor present.
options.rationale: Eleven identical reports and a rising rework trend cannot both be accurate, and only direct contact settles which is wrong. Going without the supervisor is not an accusation; it is the only arrangement in which someone can say something that contradicts him.

options.text: Ask the supervisor to expand the Friday report to cover morale and rework in more detail.
options.rationale: It asks the filter you already suspect to describe itself more thoroughly. A longer report from the same source restates the same view at greater length and takes another month to do it.

options.text: Introduce a dashboard so that rework and attrition are visible weekly.
options.rationale: Measurement would confirm a trend you have already seen without explaining any of it. Why two fitters left and why rework is rising live in conversations no dashboard has ever collected.

options.text: Circulate a morale survey to everyone on site.
options.rationale: It asks for candour from twenty-three people the project manager has almost entirely never met. Anonymous scores from strangers produce a number to worry about rather than anything specific enough to act on.

questions.explanation: A single reporting channel becomes a filter, and a filter is invisible from the far end because everything arriving through it is consistent with itself. Hard evidence that contradicts the narrative — attrition, rework, defect rates — is usually the first thing to notice, and no amount of extra reporting from the same source will resolve it. Presence where the work happens is a leadership instrument rather than a courtesy, and its value lies in the conversations that only become possible once somebody is standing there.
questions.mindset: Go to where the work is, because a report can only tell you what its author is able to say.

questions.stem: A technician on your bridge strengthening contract tells you privately that a colleague has signed off three weld inspection records for welds he did not witness. She has no evidence beyond having been on shift with him, she is a year into her career, and she asks you to keep it between the two of you because she has to work alongside him every day. Nothing has failed. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Tell her you cannot keep this one confidential, explain exactly what will happen next, and route it formally while shielding her where you can.
options.rationale: Structural inspection records are safety evidence, so this cannot stay between two people whatever was hoped. Telling her before acting preserves her trust and her willingness to speak again, and shielding her is a commitment that can actually be kept.

options.text: Agree to keep it confidential and quietly satisfy yourself by examining the three welds.
options.rationale: It honours the promise and abandons the duty. An informal look by a project manager is not an inspection, carries no standing, and disturbs the evidence trail if the concern turns out to be well founded.

options.text: Speak to the colleague directly and give him the chance to explain before taking it any further.
options.rationale: It warns the one person with a motive to alter records, and identifies the source almost immediately since only one colleague shared those shifts. Meant as fairness, it compromises both the evidence and the person who came forward.

options.text: Tell her she must raise it herself through the whistleblowing procedure if she wants it addressed.
options.rationale: It hands the risk back to the most junior person present and makes action conditional on her courage. Once told, the obligation belongs to the project manager regardless of what she chooses to do next.

questions.explanation: A promise of confidence cannot be given before the content is known, and certain categories — falsified safety evidence, harm to people, criminality — remove the option the moment they are spoken. The leadership work is not whether to act but how: saying what will happen before it happens, protecting the person from the consequences you can control, and preserving the evidence by not warning the subject. Confidentiality that cannot be honoured should never be offered, and withdrawing it afterwards costs far more than declining it at the outset.
questions.mindset: Never promise a confidence before you know what it contains, and say what you will do before you do it.

questions.stem: It is two in the morning on the cutover weekend for a hospital catering system serving four sites. The team has been working for sixteen hours. In the last hour two configuration errors have been made and caught, both by luck rather than by the checks. The rollback window closes in ninety minutes and the remaining work is estimated at two hours. Your sponsor, at home, is pressing you to push on. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Roll back now while the window is still open, and tell the sponsor the decision and the reason for it.
options.rationale: Two errors in an hour from a team sixteen hours in is the evidence that matters, and two hours of work does not fit ninety minutes even at full performance. Deciding while the safe option still exists is the entire purpose of having a window.

options.text: Push on, since the sponsor supports it and only two hours of work remain.
options.rationale: It plans the next two hours at a performance level the last hour has just disproved, and spends the rollback option to do it. A thirty-minute slip then leaves four hospital sites with no way back.

options.text: Continue, but add a second person to check every remaining step.
options.rationale: It adds a control staffed by the same exhausted people and lengthens the work it is meant to check. Fatigue degrades a checker exactly as it degrades an operator, which is why both errors were caught by luck rather than by the checks already in place.

options.text: Put the decision to the team and follow whatever the majority prefer.
options.rationale: It hands an accountable safety decision to people too tired to make it, who after sixteen hours will feel obliged to say carry on. Consulting a team is not the same as delegating to it, and this decision is the project manager's to sign.

questions.explanation: Fatigue is a project risk with an observable rate — errors per hour — and once that rate is climbing it invalidates every estimate made before it. Reversibility is an asset that expires on a clock, so the decision must be taken while the safe option still exists rather than at the moment the unsafe one fails. Part of leading under pressure is protecting both the users and the team from a choice the team is in no condition to make, and carrying the sponsor's displeasure personally rather than distributing it.
questions.mindset: Decide while the safe option is still available, and treat fatigue as evidence rather than as an excuse.

questions.stem: The chart plots your university student records squad's completed points as a line, against its recorded overtime hours as bars, across six iterations. Nobody raised a concern at the time and the team met every commitment until the last one. Select the iteration at which the leader should have intervened.

graphic.title: Completed points and recorded overtime hours across six iterations
graphic.caption: Select an iteration. Use Tab or the arrow keys to move between them, then Enter or Space.

regions.label: Iteration 2 — points steady, overtime near zero
regions.rationale: A flat iteration with no overtime is the baseline everything else on this chart should be read against. Treating ordinary variation as a warning is how leaders manufacture pressure that was not there.

regions.label: Iteration 3 — points up sharply, overtime up sharply
regions.rationale: This is the first point at which output and hours rise together, which means the gain was bought rather than earned. Acting here costs one conversation; the same conversation two iterations later costs a recovery period.

regions.label: Iteration 4 — points up slightly, overtime still high
regions.rationale: By now the pattern is established and the team has normalised the hours. It remains a reasonable moment to act, but it is not where the signal first appeared, and a month of accumulated fatigue is already priced in.

regions.label: Iteration 6 — points collapse, overtime falls away
regions.rationale: This is the consequence rather than the signal, and it is the point at which most teams first get attention. Once output falls and the hours stop, the only intervention left is recovery rather than prevention.

questions.explanation: Two series read together say something neither says alone: output and effort climbing at once means the gain was purchased with hours rather than produced by capability. The moment to act is the first divergence from the baseline, not the moment the consequence becomes visible, because by then the available options have narrowed to recovery. A leader watching only the delivery line will always intervene one cycle after the evidence was there to see.
questions.mindset: Read output against the effort that bought it, and act on the first signal rather than the first consequence.

questions.stem: The diagram shows who talks to whom on your fisheries quota system programme. Six specialists sit around a project coordinator, and the two external groups reach the team only through her. She is capable, well liked, and increasingly the person every question waits for. Select the element of this structure that presents the greatest risk to the team's ability to keep working.

graphic.title: Communication paths between six specialists, a coordinator and two external groups
graphic.caption: Select an element. Use Tab or the arrow keys to move between them, then Enter or Space.

regions.label: The coordinator at the centre, through whom every path runs
regions.rationale: Every route between specialists and every route to the outside passes through one person, so her absence halts all of them at once. A structure that concentrates every path in a capable individual is a design decision even when nobody designed it.

regions.label: A specialist at the edge holding a single link
regions.rationale: A peripheral node with one connection is a consequence of the hub rather than a cause of anything. Choosing it mistakes a symptom for the structure producing it, and fixing this node alone leaves five others identical.

regions.label: The external regulator group, connected only through the coordinator
regions.rationale: This single connection is a genuine weakness, but it is one instance of the hub's effect rather than the hub itself. Repairing this link leaves the other seven routes running through the same person.

regions.label: The direct link between two specialists that bypasses the centre
regions.rationale: This is the healthy pattern on the diagram rather than a risk: two people resolving something without routing it through anyone. The remedy for the rest of the structure is more links exactly like this one.

questions.explanation: A coordination structure has a shape, and the shape decides what happens when any one person is unavailable. Hub-and-spoke arrangements form naturally around whoever is most helpful, because routing through a capable person is easier for everyone in the short term than building the direct relationships. The leadership work is to create the missing links deliberately — introductions, shared forums, named counterparts — so that the hub becomes a convenience rather than the only road.
questions.mindset: Build direct routes between the people who need each other, rather than becoming the road they all use.

questions.stem: Your national library digitisation programme has just formed a team of thirteen drawn from four departments. Cataloguing writes everything down and expects two days' notice for any decision. Imaging decides in the corridor. Conservation escalates disagreements to its head of department by default. IT works to a formal change process. Three weeks in, each group believes the others are behaving unreasonably, and all four have said so to you separately. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Bring the four groups together to surface how each currently works, then agree one set of ways of working for this team.
options.rationale: Nobody is misbehaving; four locally rational norms are colliding and none of the groups can see the others'. Making them visible in one room turns an argument about character into a set of choices the team can negotiate.

options.text: Adopt the practices of the largest department, since most of the team already knows them.
options.rationale: It settles the question by headcount rather than by fit, and tells three departments their way of working lost a vote. It also imports norms designed for cataloguing into imaging and IT work they were never meant for.

options.text: Write a ways-of-working document yourself and issue it to the team.
options.rationale: It produces a rule set quickly and skips the part that makes rules stick. The four groups keep their habits and treat the document as the project manager's preference rather than an agreement they made.

options.text: Ask each department head to tell their people to be more flexible with the others.
options.rationale: It routes a team problem through four line managers and asks for a general attitude instead of a specific behaviour. Nothing observable changes, and the team learns that friction goes upward rather than getting resolved.

questions.explanation: When people from different parts of an organisation form a team, they arrive carrying norms that were sensible where they came from, and the resulting friction is routinely misread as unreasonableness. Surfacing the differences explicitly converts an argument about who is difficult into a set of choices, and choices a team makes are the ones it will enforce on itself. The leader supplies the forum and the insistence that one set of norms is agreed rather than four quietly tolerated.
questions.mindset: Assume colliding norms rather than difficult people, and get the differences into the open where they can be chosen between.

questions.stem: The annual engagement survey for your waste management fleet programme returns a low score on the statement about whether people feel their manager listens, and three free-text comments say meetings are dominated by the project manager. Twenty-two people responded. You are surprised, and your first instinct is that the comments come from two people you recently disagreed with. Which two actions should the project manager take?

options.text: Share the results with the team unedited and ask for specific examples of when it happens.
options.rationale: Publishing an uncomfortable result is the only way to show that the survey is safe to answer honestly. Asking for specifics also moves the feedback from a score you can dispute to a behaviour you can actually change.

options.text: Change one visible behaviour in meetings and ask the team to hold you to it.
options.rationale: A single observable commitment, such as speaking last, is testable within a fortnight and gives the team explicit permission to challenge you. It proves the feedback produced something, which decides whether next year's is answered.

options.text: Ask human resources to re-run the survey with clearer questions.
