options.rationale: It disputes the instrument rather than the finding and buys several weeks. The team reads a re-run accurately, as an attempt to obtain a better answer to the same question.

options.text: Work out who wrote the comments so that you can discuss them directly.
options.rationale: It breaks the anonymity that produced the information and guarantees nothing candid is ever submitted again. Even a correct identification leaves you addressing two people about a score twenty-two of them gave.

options.text: Explain to the team, with examples, why your level of involvement in meetings is necessary.
options.rationale: It answers feedback with justification, which reads as refusal however reasonable the examples are. The score describes how the meetings feel, and no explanation of intent changes a felt experience.

questions.explanation: Feedback about a leader is worth whatever the leader does with it in the first fortnight, and the two things that count are visibility and a change somebody else can observe. Investigating the source, disputing the method or explaining the behaviour all carry the same message — that the feedback was a problem to be managed — and each reliably reduces what the next round will tell you. The score itself is nearly useless; the specifics behind it are the entire value, and only an honest response ever produces them.
questions.mindset: Answer feedback with one observable change, because everything else teaches people not to give it.

questions.stem: Three individual behaviours on your stadium ticketing squad have started to affect other people, and in each case the team has quietly adapted around them rather than raising anything. You have decided to deal with all three this week. Complete each sentence with the response that fits. One choice is not used.

prompts.text: A developer arrives ten minutes into every stand-up, and the team has begun starting without him. The project manager should
After a disagreement with you, an engineer has started copying your manager into routine queries. The project manager should
A developer disagrees with an agreed technical direction and re-opens it in every design session. The project manager should

options.text: raise it with him privately and this week, before the workaround becomes the norm
options.rationale: The team has already absorbed the behaviour, which is why nobody will mention it and why it will spread. Small, early and private is the cheapest form this conversation ever takes.

options.text: address it with her face to face rather than answering through the copied channel
options.rationale: Replying in the thread accepts the escalation as the new medium and invites your manager into a two-person problem. The behaviour is about the disagreement, and that is the conversation still owed.

options.text: give the disagreement one full hearing, then hold the decision and say plainly that it is closed
options.rationale: Re-litigating a settled direction costs the whole group time and signals that decisions are provisional. A proper hearing earns the right to close it, and closing it is what the rest of the team needs.

options.text: ask the team to raise it with the individual at the next retrospective
options.rationale: Not used. A retrospective examines the team's system of work rather than one person's conduct, and putting any of these three in front of the group converts a correctable behaviour into a public judgement.

questions.explanation: Teams adapt around individual behaviour rather than confronting it, which is why the leader is usually the last to hear and always the right person to act. Each of these needs a direct conversation, and what differs is the venue and the timing rather than the courage required. Behaviour that the group has already worked around has passed the point where it corrects itself, and the cost of raising it only ever rises.
questions.mindset: When a team has quietly worked around someone's behaviour, the conversation is already overdue and it is yours to have.

questions.stem: An engineer on your greenhouse automation project tells you his father has been admitted to hospital and the situation is serious. He says he wants to carry on exactly as normal. The next fortnight is the busiest of the project and he owns the irrigation controller integration, which nobody else has touched. He is visibly holding himself together as he tells you. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Say what you are changing to take pressure off, then ask what would help, and re-plan the fortnight so he is not carrying it alone.
options.rationale: Somebody in the first days of a crisis is the worst-placed person to judge their own capacity, and an open question invites him to say he is fine. Leading with what you will change gives him permission he cannot ask for.

options.text: Respect his wishes and let him continue as normal, checking in at the end of the fortnight.
options.rationale: It treats a sentence spoken under acute stress as a considered judgement about capacity, and sets the check for a point after the risk has either passed or landed. Autonomy is a sound principle applied here at the wrong moment.

options.text: Sign him off for the fortnight and redistribute the integration work immediately.
options.rationale: It removes his choice entirely and takes away work that may be the one stable thing he has. Deciding for someone is not the same as supporting them, and he may genuinely need to be here.

options.text: Tell the team quietly what has happened so that they can cover for him discreetly.
options.rationale: It shares his private circumstances without asking and organises sympathy behind his back. Whatever the intent, he loses control of who knows, and discovers he has lost it when someone is unexpectedly kind.

questions.explanation: A person in crisis cannot reliably assess their own capacity, and asking whether they need anything produces a refusal, because accepting help means admitting the situation. The workable sequence is to change something concrete first and ask second, so the choice in front of them is whether to accept relief rather than whether to request it. The delivery exposure is real and is handled by re-planning around a single point of dependency, which was a risk before any of this happened.
questions.mindset: Offer the change first and the question second, because people in crisis decline what they are asked to request.

questions.stem: An audit of where your ceramics manufacturer's planning system team spends its week shows fourteen hours a person in meetings, out of thirty-seven. You called eleven of the fifteen recurring meetings yourself and governance requires three of the others. Two engineers have told you, carefully, that they do their real work in the evenings. Which two actions should the project manager take?

options.text: Review the eleven meetings you own and cancel or shorten the ones that exist mainly to keep you informed.
options.rationale: The largest single contributor is the leader's own appetite for information, and it is the part that can be cut this week without anyone's permission. Auditing your own load first is also what makes any later request of governance credible.

options.text: Give the team a protected block each week in which no meeting may be scheduled, and defend it.
options.rationale: Uninterrupted time is the resource being consumed, and it only exists if somebody holds the line against future requests. Declaring the block is easy; defending it against the next urgent invitation is the leadership part.

options.text: Ask the team to decline the meetings they consider optional.
options.rationale: It pushes the decision down to people who cannot see which meetings matter politically and who will pay for guessing wrong. They keep attending, and now believe the lost time is their own fault.

options.text: Shorten every meeting to twenty-five minutes to recover time across the board.
options.rationale: It applies a uniform trim to meetings with entirely different purposes and leaves the week just as fragmented. Fifteen shorter interruptions are barely better than fifteen longer ones for work that needs a run at it.

options.text: Ask governance to reduce its three required meetings before touching your own.
options.rationale: It begins with the meetings you neither control nor can cut, which delays any change and spends credibility to do it. It also asks others to give up time while your own eleven remain untouched.

questions.explanation: Meeting load is a leadership output before it is a team problem: most of it is created by whoever is trying to stay informed, and the cost falls on people whose work needs continuous time. Cutting your own first is both the largest available saving and the only thing that makes a wider request legitimate. Fragmentation matters as much as the total, which is why a protected block beats trimming every meeting by a few minutes.
questions.mindset: Audit the demands you make on the team's time before asking anyone else to reduce theirs.

questions.stem: Sprint planning on your bus operator's driver app routinely runs to four hours for a two-week sprint, and ends with the team tired and the plan thin. People arrive without having looked at the upcoming items, and refinement, which was supposed to run mid-sprint, has not happened since March. Your delivery manager has suggested capping planning at ninety minutes. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Restore mid-sprint refinement first, and let the length of planning fall as a consequence.
options.rationale: Planning runs long because thinking that belonged earlier is happening here instead. Repairing the upstream session shortens the meeting on its own, which is the only version of the change that lasts past the first busy sprint.

options.text: Cap planning at ninety minutes as suggested and hold the team to the limit.
options.rationale: It removes the visible symptom and keeps the cause, so the team leaves with a plan built on items nobody has examined. The cost simply moves from a long meeting into a poor sprint, where it is much harder to see.

options.text: Prepare the plan yourself in advance and bring it to the session for the team to confirm.
options.rationale: It fixes a four-hour meeting by removing the team from the planning of its own work. Attendance improves, ownership does not, and the estimates quietly become yours to defend.

options.text: Extend the sprint to four weeks so that planning happens half as often.
options.rationale: It halves the frequency of the pain and doubles the distance between feedback points. The unexamined items remain unexamined; there are simply more of them in each conversation.

questions.explanation: A meeting that overruns is usually doing work that belongs upstream of it, and capping the meeting relocates the failure rather than removing it. The diagnostic question is what the session is being asked to produce that it was never designed to produce — here, a first examination of items that should have been understood days earlier. Repair the upstream activity and the downstream symptom resolves without anybody having to enforce a timer.
questions.mindset: When a meeting overruns, look upstream for the work it is doing on somebody else's behalf.

questions.stem: Your pharmaceutical packaging programme runs in a matrix. Annual reviews are written by functional managers, none of whom has seen your team's project work for a year. One of your strongest performers has just been rated as meeting expectations, on a form her manager completed without asking you for anything. Two other team members have noticed, and one has asked whether project work counts for anything at all. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Ask for her rating to be reconsidered with your evidence, and agree with all the functional managers how project input reaches every review in future.
options.rationale: The individual case needs correcting and the route needs building, and only the second stops this recurring for the other twelve. Raising both together also frames it as a process gap rather than an attack on one manager's judgement.

options.text: Raise it with her functional manager as a complaint about this particular rating.
options.rationale: It contests one case and leaves the mechanism intact, so the same thing happens to somebody else next year. Framing a systemic gap as a personal disagreement is also the version most likely to be defended against.

options.text: Tell her privately that you rate her work highly and will recognise it inside the project.
options.rationale: Private reassurance from someone with no say in the rating counts for little against a written record, and the record is what follows her. It also confirms her colleague's suspicion that project work carries no formal weight.

options.text: Accept it, since performance ratings are a line management matter outside the project manager's authority.
options.rationale: It treats the absence of formal authority as the end of the question, when influence over the input was available throughout. The team then draws the accurate conclusion that a year of project work is invisible where it counts.

questions.explanation: In a matrix the people doing the work are appraised by managers who did not see it, and that gap is a structural feature rather than an oversight, which means somebody has to close it deliberately and in advance. A project manager with no authority over ratings still controls the evidence reaching them, and supplying it systematically for the whole team beats contesting individual outcomes after the event. Where a team concludes that its project contribution is invisible to the people deciding pay and promotion, the discretionary effort leaves with that conclusion.
questions.mindset: You may not own the rating, but you own the evidence that reaches it — supply it for everyone, in advance.

questions.stem: During the commissioning review of your waste-to-energy plant, a technician mentions that three weeks ago he noticed a valve line-up he believed was wrong and said nothing, because a senior engineer had already signed the sheet. He was right; somebody else caught it four hours later and corrected it before start-up. Nothing was damaged and no report was raised at the time. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Treat the silence as the finding: thank him where the team can see it, and work out with them what would have made speaking up easy.
options.rationale: The valve was corrected, so the risk still live is the deference that stopped a correct observation being voiced. Making the response to speaking up visibly positive is the only intervention that reaches the next person who hesitates.

options.text: Thank him privately and remind the team that anyone may raise a concern at any time.
options.rationale: A private thank-you leaves everyone else holding the belief they already have, which is that challenging a signature is not done. A general reminder costs nothing and changes nothing, because the barrier was never ignorance of the rule.

options.text: Add a second signature to the valve line-up procedure so that the error is caught by process.
options.rationale: It adds a control against a technical error that was already caught, and does nothing about the authority gradient that suppressed a correct observation. Two signatures also dilute the responsibility each signatory feels.

options.text: Speak to the senior engineer about the error on the sheet he signed.
options.rationale: It addresses the technical mistake and confirms precisely the dynamic in question, since the junior technician's account becomes a report about a senior colleague. The next observation is even less likely to be voiced.

questions.explanation: A near miss carries two findings — the technical fault, and whatever stopped it being raised — and the second usually matters more because it will apply to the next fault as well. Where the barrier is seniority, procedural additions do not touch it; only a visible and positive response to someone challenging a senior person changes the calculation for the next observer. What a team reads is what happened to the last person who spoke, which is why the response has to be public to be read at all.
questions.mindset: Treat whatever stopped someone speaking as the real finding, and answer it where everyone can see.

questions.stem: Funding is moving and your public broadcaster's archive product squad will be broken up in six weeks. You learned this on Tuesday. Yesterday a developer asked you about a slide she had seen in a portfolio pack showing the squad ending, and three others have since asked her what she knows. The formal announcement is scheduled for a fortnight's time. Which two actions should the project manager take?

options.text: Tell the team what you know now, separating what is settled from what is not and when the rest will be decided.
options.rationale: They already know something is happening, so the real choice is between a version from you and a version from a slide. Separating the settled from the undecided is what stops rumour filling a fortnight of silence.

options.text: Give people something they can control, such as where they would like to move and what they want finished first.
options.rationale: Most of the distress in an ending comes from having no agency in it, and both of these are real choices you can influence. It also turns six weeks of drift into work that has a point.

options.text: Wait for the formal announcement so that everybody hears the same message at the same time.
options.rationale: The simultaneous message was already lost to a portfolio slide. A fortnight of visible silence from a leader who plainly knows costs far more trust than an imperfect early briefing would.

options.text: Reassure the team that nothing is decided and the funding position may still change.
options.rationale: It buys calm with a claim you cannot support, and the correction arrives in two weeks with your credibility attached to it. People make plans on reassurance, which is what makes it expensive.

options.text: Keep the team focused on the remaining scope and address the ending once it is formally confirmed.
options.rationale: It asks people to concentrate on a backlog while the question of their next job is open, which is not how attention works. Output falls anyway, and now without anyone acknowledging the reason.

questions.explanation: Endings are led rather than merely announced, and the leadership work starts when the information exists rather than when a process permits its release. Two things reduce the damage: an honest account that distinguishes the settled from the undecided, and the return of some agency over what happens next. Waiting for a formal announcement makes sense only where nobody has heard anything, and once a team is asking questions that condition has already gone.
questions.mindset: Lead an ending from the moment you know, and give people back whatever choices remain.
